title: ExxonMobil Earnings Beat Estimates as Refining Margins Lift Profit to $15.4 Billion, Revenue Rises 32.7%
excerpt: Adjusted EPS of $4.23 topped the $3.90 consensus and revenue beat by nearly 10%, as record refining margins made ExxonMobil's fuels business out-earn its oil production.
body:
• ExxonMobil's third-quarter profit more than doubled to $15.4 billion, or $3.72 per share; adjusted earnings of $4.23 per share beat the Zacks consensus of $3.90 by 8.5%.
  • Revenue rose 32.7% to $113.16 billion, topping the $103 billion consensus, as record refining margins drove adjusted Energy Products earnings of $9.05 billion — refining out-earned the upstream business.
  • The company generated $25.7 billion of operating cash flow and $19.1 billion of free cash flow, returned $9.4 billion to shareholders, and cut net debt to $22.1 billion.
  • ExxonMobil declared a fourth-quarter dividend of $1.07 per share and announced $20 billion of share repurchases planned for 2027.

ExxonMobil reported third-quarter 2026 earnings that more than doubled from a year earlier, the company announced Friday in its official results release, as a surge in refining margins more than offset softer crude prices. Earnings under U.S. GAAP were $15.4 billion, or $3.72 per share, up from $7.55 billion, or $1.76 per share, in the same quarter last year. Adjusted earnings were $17.5 billion, or $4.23 per share.

Refining does the heavy lifting

On the adjusted measures Wall Street tracks, the quarter was a clear beat: the $4.23 per share topped the Zacks Consensus Estimate of $3.90 by 8.5%, and revenue of $113.16 billion beat the $103 billion consensus by 9.9%, rising 32.7% from $85.29 billion a year ago. The unusual feature of the quarter was where the money was made. Adjusted earnings from Energy Products — the refining and fuels business — reached $9.05 billion, with segment sales of 5,753 thousand barrels per day, on record refining margins and strong diesel yields. On a GAAP basis, Energy Products earned $7.17 billion, edging past the upstream production business's $7.09 billion — a rare inversion for a company whose fortunes are usually tied to the wellhead.

Upstream adjusted earnings were $7.31 billion. The GAAP figure slipped from the second quarter's $7.93 billion on lower oil prices and an accelerated production-entitlement effect in Guyana, while worldwide production held broadly steady at about 4.5 million oil-equivalent barrels per day. Chemical Products was the soft spot, with adjusted earnings falling to $725 million from $1.2 billion as margins weakened.

Cash flow funds returns and a cleaner balance sheet

Cash flow from operating activities was $25.7 billion and free cash flow was $19.1 billion in the quarter. ExxonMobil returned $9.4 billion to shareholders — $4.3 billion of dividends and $5.1 billion of share repurchases — and said it plans a further $20 billion of buybacks in 2027, subject to market conditions. The board declared a fourth-quarter dividend of $1.07 per share, payable December 10, 2026, to shareholders of record on November 16.

The quarter also built on the second quarter rather than merely beating a weak year-ago comparison: GAAP earnings rose $888 million from the second quarter's $14.5 billion, and adjusted earnings rose $2.8 billion sequentially. For the first nine months of 2026, reported EPS reached $8.18 and adjusted EPS $9.82, against $5.16 and $5.19, respectively, in the same period of 2025 — a step-change in profitability that the company has attributed to years of investment in advantaged assets and cost discipline.

The balance sheet strengthened further. Net debt fell to $22.1 billion at September 30 — $34.3 billion of total debt less $12.2 billion of cash — a reduction of nearly $11 billion since the start of the year. Year-to-date earnings reached $34.1 billion, against $22.3 billion in the first nine months of 2025, putting the largest U.S. oil company on course for one of its strongest years on record even as crude prices eased from their second-quarter levels.
